title: Sleeping with the Fishes
victoryHeadline: Caught! Erin's breathing exercise finally gave her away.
acts: The harbour at Cortown ran on tides, tea breaks, and Vincenza's twice-yearly safety inspection, which she carried out every spring and autumn with a clipboard, a spirit level, and zero patience for a loose plank. That afternoon she worked her way along the boards, muttering measurements to herself, past a woman in a folding chair who'd been sitting very still, rocking gently, breathing in for four and out for six — ostensibly readying herself for a job interview nobody else on the harbour knew about. Vincenza barely registered her going past. Erin barely registered Vincenza. The tide, unbothered by either of them, kept doing what it always did.

Out on the water, Antonio had finally decided to learn to row properly, technique video memorised twice over, and was now twenty minutes into an extremely committed, entirely involuntary circle. "You're going the WRONG WAY," Claire bellowed helpfully from the other boat, feet up, sunhat on, savouring the first afternoon off she'd had in a month. "I KNOW," Antonio bellowed back, and kept going the wrong way. Down on Dock B, Franklin — fedora, good suit, thoroughly unsuited to fieldwork — had his phone angled at a cormorant for a birdwatching forum that had no idea what he did for a living, while Graham stood hooded and masked beside a crate of ice bound for his sister's wedding cake two docks over, sniffling gently behind a mask that had nothing to do with anyone but his own hay fever. Their shouting carried further across the water than either of them realised, which turned out, as it happened, to be rather useful to somebody.

Inland, the Fish Market was running its own quiet war. Barry sat in his chair by the front box, keeping the tally he kept every single day: whoever shorted a customer on ice first, lost. Delilah, eighty and entirely unbothered, was already two ahead, weighing sprats to the exact gram and refusing, on principle, to round anything in anyone's favour. In the Warehouse, Hilton worked the shelves alone in a suit built for a christening, counting tins of pilchards and quietly regretting his own personal definition of 'smart casual.' Then a short, sharp sound carried across the harbour and was gone almost at once, lost under all that shouting from the water. It took a good ten minutes, and an abandoned clipboard sitting closed on a bench, before anyone thought to walk the length of the boards and check.

whereabouts.A: Antonio had taken the rowboat out to finally learn how to row, following a technique video he'd watched twice, and after twenty minutes had succeeded only in going in a very committed, very consistent circle.
whereabouts.B: Barry sat in his usual chair by the fish market's front box, keeping his running tally of which stallholder shorted a customer on ice first today — Delilah was already two ahead and it wasn't even lunchtime.
whereabouts.C: Claire had swapped shifts to take the other boat out for the first proper afternoon off she'd had in a month, shouting increasingly elaborate updates on her tan to Antonio, who was too busy going in circles to answer.
whereabouts.D: Delilah stood beside her crate weighing out sprats to the gram, refusing, as a matter of ancient principle, to round anything in the customer's favour.
whereabouts.E: Erin had pulled a folding chair to the end of the Boardwalk and was going through her breathing exercises before a job interview she hadn't told anyone about, rocking gently on the back legs and timing each breath to the tide.
whereabouts.F: Franklin stood on Dock B in his good suit and fedora, phone held at an odd angle, trying to get a clean photo of a cormorant for the birdwatching forum where nobody knew his actual job.
whereabouts.G: Graham stood hooded, masked and wrapped up like a man expecting weather, guarding a crate of ice for his sister's wedding cake two docks over — the mask was for his pollen allergy, and for nobody's benefit but his own sinuses.
whereabouts.H: Hilton worked the Warehouse shelves in a suit built for a christening, not a stock check, having been assured that morning it was 'smart casual enough' for counting tins of pilchards.
whereabouts.V: Vincenza walked the Boardwalk boards with a clipboard of her own, doing the harbour's twice-yearly safety inspection and muttering about a loose plank she kept meaning to finally report.

reveal: It was Erin, on the Boardwalk — and the breathing exercises were entirely real, just not for the reason anyone assumed. She'd spent the whole afternoon walking that folding chair back, inch by patient inch, into exactly the right spot beside the one plank Vincenza had flagged on every inspection for six years running and nobody had ever fixed. When Vincenza finally crouched down to replace it herself, Erin leaned back one last time and let the chair's rocking do what six years of neglect had been quietly asking for: the plank flipped, Vincenza went into the harbour with barely a sound over Claire's shouting, and Erin closed the chair, gathered her things, and went off to her very real, and subsequently successful, job interview. Vincenza, harbour tradition now insists, is sleeping with the fishes.

escape.generic: The case went cold, the loose plank finally got fixed, and the real killer breezed through the job interview without a single follow-up question about her afternoon.

byAccused.A: Antonio was taken in still holding the oars, and to this day maintains — loudly, to anyone who'll listen — that another five minutes would have cracked it.
byAccused.B: "I notice things," Barry said, more than once, as they walked him out of the market. "I would have noticed a murder." Nobody had a good answer, and it didn't save him.
byAccused.C: The papers ran a photo of Claire's boat, empty, feet-marks still visible on the bow, and half the harbour spent months convinced she'd been sunbathing her way through a criminal empire; she had, in fact, just wanted the day off.
byAccused.D: Delilah's sprats went unweighed for a week, and the Fish Market's ice count has never fully recovered from the loss of the only person keeping anyone honest.
byAccused.F: The birdwatching forum posted a brief, baffled tribute to a member they'd known only as 'DockBirder92', unaware he'd been arrested two docks over for a murder he'd been too busy photographing a cormorant to notice.
byAccused.G: Graham was hauled off still masked, still hooded, still insisting — muffled, sniffling — that the crate really was just ice for a wedding cake, which it was, and which nobody at the station believed for a second.
byAccused.H: Hilton's pilchard count was left one christening-suit sleeve short of finished, and the Warehouse has run on a wrong number ever since.
